openingProblem.problem: In 1979 revolutionaries overthrew a corrupt dictator in a small Central American country. For the next decade the United States funded a guerrilla war against them, and a scandal over that funding shook the White House. Why did Nicaragua become a Cold War battleground, and how did the war end?

openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Revolution: the fall of Somoza, 1977–1979
chunks.body:
For over forty years Nicaragua was ruled by one family, the Somozas, close allies of the United States. Anastasio Somoza García ruled from 1936 to 1956, his son Luis until 1966, and then Anastasio Somoza, who controlled the country's politics, army and much of its economy. Public anger exploded after an earthquake struck the capital, Managua, in 1972: Somoza's businesses, cronies and officers stole most of the international relief money.

Opposition grew on two fronts. The middle class, business leaders and the Catholic Church became increasingly critical of Somoza. Meanwhile a committed group of revolutionaries, inspired by the Cuban revolution of 1959 and advised by Fidel Castro, founded the **Sandinista National Liberation Front** (FSLN), named after Augusto Sandino, who had fought US Marines in the 1920s. In January 1978 the opposition newspaper publisher Pedro Joaquín Chamorro was assassinated, and the country slid into civil war. In August 1978 Sandinista guerrillas seized the National Palace; in September they attacked major cities.

President **Jimmy Carter** faced a dilemma. In 1977 he had promised a foreign policy based on human rights and an end to US intervention in Latin America, and Somoza's dictatorship was exactly what he opposed. But the Cold War, in the Office of the Historian's words, turned his policy into "a torturous balancing act". Carter criticised Somoza but would not encourage the Sandinistas, because of their Cuban ties and the Marxism of their leaders. He tried to engineer a middle way. An OAS mediation in late 1978 failed to persuade Somoza to accept free elections, and in January 1979 he rejected a supervised plebiscite. In February 1979 Carter cut off military aid to Somoza's National Guard and asked other countries to stop aiding the Sandinistas.

Events moved faster than Washington. In June 1979 a Provisional Government of Sandinistas and moderates was formed in Costa Rica, and the OAS called for Somoza's replacement. Somoza fled to the United States on 17 July, and on **19 July 1979** Sandinista forces entered Managua.

This mattered because a local revolution against a corrupt dictator brought Marxist revolutionaries with Cuban links to power in Central America, which meant that Nicaragua became a Cold War issue for the United States.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The revolution also had broad moderate support.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Carter's balancing act failed to produce a moderate transition.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Somoza's refusal to compromise blocked every plan.

chunks.title: From Carter to Reagan: the Contras, 1979–1982
chunks.body:
At first Carter tried to influence the new government rather than oppose it. In September 1979 he met members of the Sandinista-led Government of National Reconstruction at the White House and urged moderation and respect for human rights. After a long debate, Congress authorised $80 million for Central America in May 1980, with conditions: six-monthly reports on human rights in Nicaragua, and an end to aid if foreign forces there threatened US security or its allies.

The region was becoming more violent. In neighbouring **El Salvador**, a reforming junta faced attacks from left and right; Archbishop Oscar Romero was murdered, and in December 1980 four American churchwomen were killed, with the involvement of the security forces. In January 1981 the leftist guerrillas of the FMLN launched a major offensive.

**Ronald Reagan**, elected in November 1980, saw Central America as a front line of the Cold War. In February 1981 the State Department issued a White Paper claiming that Cuba and other Communist states had played a central role in arming the Salvadoran rebels. Secretary of State Alexander Haig accused the Sandinistas of exporting terrorism to El Salvador, and in April 1981 Reagan ended economic aid to Nicaragua. More broadly, Reagan's policy was to roll back Communism in Latin America, Africa and South Asia.

After diplomatic efforts to stop Nicaraguan support for the Salvadoran rebels failed, Reagan backed a clandestine guerrilla force, the **Contras** ("counter-revolutionaries"). Most were former members of Somoza's National Guard, gathered across the border in Honduras. They launched their first major attack in March 1982. The Sandinistas responded with a dramatic military build-up, assisted by Soviet and Cuban advisers and armed mostly with Soviet-bloc weapons.

This mattered because American fear of Communist expansion turned a domestic revolution into a proxy war, which meant that Nicaragua became a battleground in which each superpower bloc armed one side.

chunks.title: The Contra war, Congress and Iran-Contra, 1982–1986
chunks.body:
Reagan's support for the Contras met resistance at home. Many in Congress feared that the US was being drawn into a war to overthrow the Sandinistas, or even into direct military involvement. In December 1982 Congress passed legislation, sponsored by Representative Edward Boland, that banned the use of US funds to overthrow the Sandinista government, while still allowing aid to the Contras for other purposes.

Reagan kept pressing. In April 1983 he told Congress that the Sandinista government threatened Central America and the security of the United States. American military exercises off Nicaragua's coast and the US invasion of Grenada in October 1983 showed his determination, and the Sandinistas agreed to take part in the **Contadora** peace talks begun in January 1983 by Mexico, Venezuela, Colombia and Panama. Congress allowed up to $100 million in non-military aid. But in October 1984, after learning that Nicaraguan harbours had been mined and an oil facility destroyed, Congress ended support for the Contras. In November 1984 Reagan was re-elected, and the Sandinista leader **Daniel Ortega** became president in a controversial election.

In his second term Reagan redoubled his commitment. In his State of the Union address of 1985 he called the Contras "freedom-fighters" defying "Soviet-supported aggression". Congress agreed $27 million in humanitarian aid in June 1985, and in 1986, after Sandinista victories and an incursion into Honduras, approved $100 million, seventy per cent of it for military aid, to be delivered in October 1986.

Then came scandal. In November 1986 the **Iran-Contra** affair broke. The Tower Commission reported that White House staff had secretly used money from arms sales to Iran and from foreign donors to arm the Contras, before Congress had approved military aid. Reagan's administration had evaded the limits Congress had set.

This mattered because the Contra war showed the limits of a president's power to fight a Cold War proxy war without public and congressional support, which meant that by 1987 the Contras' future depended on politics in Washington as much as on fighting in Nicaragua.

chunks.title: Peace and elections, 1987–1990
chunks.body:
By the late 1980s Central America had suffered hundreds of thousands of deaths and a decade of economic devastation. Regional leaders took the initiative. Building on the Contadora talks, the presidents of Central America signed a peace accord at **Esquipulas**, Guatemala, in August 1987, shaped mainly by the Costa Rican president **Óscar Arias**. It focused on democratisation and regional security, with a system of verification. In January 1988 the leaders confirmed their commitment. Ortega opened negotiations with the Contras, and the United States began to shift its aid to humanitarian purposes.

Nicaragua then held internationally supervised elections in **1990**. The winner was **Violeta Chamorro**, a former member of the revolutionary Provisional Government and the widow of Pedro Joaquín Chamorro, whose murder in 1978 had sparked the civil war. The Contras disbanded.

Did the US achieve its aims? Reagan's stated aim was to stop Nicaragua from exporting revolution and to resist "Soviet-supported aggression"; his opponents in Congress suspected the real aim was to overthrow the Sandinistas. By 1990 the Sandinistas had lost power, which Reagan's supporters saw as vindication. But they lost it in an election, under a peace process led by Central Americans rather than Washington, after the Contras had failed to defeat them militarily, and after the Iran-Contra scandal had damaged the Reagan administration.

Washington continued to see threats in Central America even as the Cold War ended: in December 1989 President Bush sent over twenty thousand troops into Panama to arrest its leader, Manuel Noriega.

This mattered because the Nicaraguan crisis was resolved by regional diplomacy and elections rather than by military victory, which meant that the outcome Washington wanted came through means it had not chosen.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: US pressure and aid cuts also shaped Sandinista choices.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Contras had failed to remove them by force.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the conflict was settled by elections rather than by military victory, so the Contras could disband.

Carter would not encourage the FSLN because of its Cuban ties, and Reagan, citing a 1981 White Paper on Communist arms for El Salvador, ended aid and backed the Contras.
This meant that a local revolution was treated as a Cold War threat, so by 1982 the Contras and a Soviet-assisted Sandinista army were at war.
However, Carter also cut military aid to Somoza in February 1979 for human rights reasons, and Congress repeatedly limited Reagan's policy.
Cold War fear was therefore the main driver, though human rights and congressional restraint shaped how far it went.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Reagan's support for the Contras achieved its aims.” Discuss with reference to the period 1981 to 1990.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim: the Contra policy succeeded
decodeKey.judgement: Which aims, and by what means?

modelPlan.thesis: The Sandinistas did lose power in 1990, but through a regional peace process and elections rather than the Contras' military campaign, and at the price of the Iran-Contra scandal, so the aim was reached by means Reagan had not chosen.

arguments.claim: For: the Sandinistas left power in 1990.
For: pressure pushed the Sandinistas to negotiate.
Against: no military victory; Congress limited the war.
Against: Iran-Contra and the human cost.

modelPlan.counter: The Sandinistas joined the Contadora talks after the Grenada invasion, suggesting US pressure worked.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By outcome, partly; by method, no.

segments.text: Reagan's Contra policy achieved its outcome but not by its chosen means.
The Sandinistas lost the internationally supervised election of 1990, but only after the Esquipulas accord of 1987, shaped by Arias, and after the Contras had failed to defeat them.
This meant that political pressure and regional diplomacy, not military victory, removed the Sandinistas from power.
However, US pressure may have pushed the Sandinistas to negotiate, as their joining the Contadora talks after the Grenada invasion of 1983 suggests.
The claim is therefore only partly valid, and the policy's cost, from Iran-Contra to hundreds of thousands of deaths in the region, was very high.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the role of the US Congress in the Contra War between 1982 and 1986.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far Congress shaped the war

modelPlan.thesis: Congress played a decisive role in limiting the methods of Reagan's policy, through the Boland legislation and the 1984 aid cut, but it also approved $100 million in 1986, so it restrained rather than stopped the war.

arguments.claim: The 1984 cut after the harbour mining.

modelPlan.counter: Reagan's administration evaded Congress through secret funding, which limits how far Congress controlled the war.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did Congress stop the war? No; it shaped it, and its limits led to Iran-Contra.

segments.text: Congress shaped the Contra war by limiting its methods rather than ending it.
In December 1982 the Boland legislation banned US funds for overthrowing the Sandinistas, and in October 1984 Congress ended support after the harbour mining.
This meant that Reagan's policy lacked secure funding, so White House staff secretly used money from arms sales to Iran.
However, Congress approved $100 million in 1986, seventy per cent military, so it did not consistently oppose the war.
Congress's role was therefore important but inconsistent, and its limits produced the scandal that discredited the policy.

essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the Nicaraguan revolution of 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The revolution was caused by the corruption and repression of the Somoza dictatorship and the failure of every plan for a moderate transition; its main consequence was a decade-long proxy war as the US backed the Contras.

arguments.claim: Cause: failed mediation and the cut in US aid.

modelPlan.counter: The FSLN's Cuban links shaped the consequences more than the causes.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The Contra war, which ended only with the 1990 election.

segments.text: The revolution was caused above all by the corruption and repression of the Somoza dictatorship.
Somoza's cronies embezzled relief after the 1972 earthquake, and the murder of Chamorro in January 1978 set off a civil war that ended when Sandinista forces entered Managua on 19 July 1979.
This meant that a broad coalition turned against Somoza, but because the FSLN had Cuban links, the revolution became a Cold War issue.
However, Carter at first tried to engage the new government, approving $80 million for the region in May 1980.
The revolution's most significant consequence was therefore Reagan's Contra war, which turned Nicaragua into a proxy battleground.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the policies of Carter and Reagan towards Nicaragua between 1979 and 1988.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked

modelPlan.thesis: Both presidents feared Sandinista links with Cuba, but Carter tried to moderate the revolution through human rights pressure and conditional aid, whereas Reagan sought to defeat it by backing the Contras.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both faced limits from Congress.

modelPlan.counter: Carter too refused to encourage the Sandinistas because of their Cuban ties, so both policies were shaped by Cold War fear.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Means: Carter sought influence, Reagan sought defeat.

segments.text: Carter and Reagan both feared Cuban influence in Nicaragua, but they chose opposite methods.
Carter met the new government in September 1979 and sought conditional aid, whereas Reagan ended aid in April 1981 and backed the Contras, who attacked in March 1982.
This meant that Carter tried to moderate the revolution from within, while Reagan tried to defeat it from outside.
However, both faced congressional limits: Carter's aid carried human rights conditions, and Reagan's was restricted by the Boland legislation.
The decisive difference was therefore between engagement and confrontation, reflecting Carter's human rights policy and Reagan's rollback.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons for the end of the Contra War between 1986 and 1990.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Reasons for the end of the war
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The war ended because the Iran-Contra scandal weakened US support, Central American leaders built the Esquipulas peace process, and supervised elections in 1990 offered a political solution that the Contras accepted by disbanding.

arguments.claim: Negotiations and the shift to humanitarian aid.

modelPlan.counter: The human and economic devastation of the war made all sides ready to end it.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? The Esquipulas process, because it provided the framework for negotiation and elections.

segments.text: The Contra war ended mainly because Central American leaders created a peace process that both sides accepted.
The Esquipulas accord of August 1987, shaped by Arias, focused on democratisation and verification, and in 1990 Chamorro won supervised elections.
This meant that the conflict could be settled by votes rather than victory, so the Contras disbanded.
However, the Iran-Contra scandal of November 1986 had already weakened US support, and the US shifted to humanitarian aid.
Regional diplomacy was therefore the main reason, made possible by the collapse of Washington's military commitment.
